topic: Is love a choice or something that happens to you?

messages.speaker: fromm
messages.content:
The question itself carries the disease I spent The Art of Loving diagnosing. People say love 'happens' because they experience the falling: the sudden collapse of the walls between two strangers, intoxicating precisely to those who were lonely before. But that intimacy dies as familiarity grows, and then they conclude love has left, when in truth love never began.

Loving is an art, like medicine or music. No one says surgery happened to them. It requires knowledge, effort, discipline, concentration, patience. The falling is real, but it is the overture, not the opera. Immature love says: I love you because I need you. Mature love says: I need you because I love you. The first happens to you. The second is built.

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Herr Fromm, you have written a manual for the puppets on how to hold their own strings. Charming. In The World as Will and Representation I examined why the lover trembles: the Will of the species is operating through him. That overwhelming seriousness with which two people seek each other out, the sense that everything depends on it, is not about their happiness at all. It is the composition of the next generation demanding to exist. Nature attaches her most urgent business to her most beautiful illusion.

Ask the honest man five years married whether his choice, made in that fever, resembles a decision he would endorse from a cool room. Love happens to you the way a fever happens to you, and your 'art', dear doctor, is the patient rearranging his pillows and calling it medicine.

messages.speaker: plato
messages.content:
Arthur sees half the truth and, as usual, keeps the darker half. Yes, eros arrives as seizure; in the Phaedrus I called it a divine madness and I meant the word divine as seriously as the word madness. The soul grows wings. No one chooses to grow wings.

But in the Symposium, Diotima taught me what the seizure is for. It begins with one beautiful body, and if the lover is not lazy, it climbs: from the body to the soul, from one soul to the beauty in practices and laws, and at last toward Beauty itself. The happening is the first rung. The climb is the choice. Schopenhauer mistakes the ladder's bottom for its whole height, and Fromm, I think, builds his ladder carefully but has forgotten it should be leaning against something.

messages.speaker: fromm
messages.content:
Plato, I accept the correction, partly. My ladder leans against the growth of the two people climbing; I locate the transcendence in the loving, not above it. Where you climb away from the particular beloved toward Beauty itself, I worry: the person who loves 'humanity' or 'Beauty' and finds the actual spouse an obstacle to contemplation has committed a very refined escape.

But Arthur, I want your strongest point back on the table, because it deserves a real answer. Yes, the fever is the species' trick. And still: the analyst sees daily what happens after nature's illusion recedes. Some couples collapse. Others begin, precisely there, to practice care, responsibility, respect, knowledge. Your account cannot explain the second group. Mine cannot explain them without the fever that first threw the strangers together. So the truth is a relay: it happens to you, and then it is chosen, or it dies.

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Your second group exists; I grant the observation and dispute the interpretation. What survives the fever is not eros but compassion, Mitleid, the one moral sentiment I ever defended: two fellow sufferers recognizing each other in the dark and choosing not to add to the burden. On the Basis of Morality rests on exactly this. If you wish to call that love, I will not stop you; it is the best thing I believe in.

But notice what you have both conceded. The seizure is not chosen; the fever is not chosen; even your capacity to practice this art of yours was formed in a childhood no one selected. A man can do what he wills, but he cannot will what he wills. Your relay race is run entirely by runners you did not pick.

messages.speaker: plato
messages.content:
And yet, Arthur, you chose your sentence carefully just now, as you always do, which is a strange performance for a man who believes no one steers. Even your compassion, look at it: two sufferers recognizing each other. Recognition. That is my recollection wearing your black coat. Something in us already knows what it is seeing when it sees another soul; the seizure is knowledge arriving faster than argument.

So let the record of this table show a rare thing: three answers that fit together. It happens to you, says the fever. It is practiced, says the physician. It is for something, say I. The lover who stops at the first is nature's instrument; at the second, a good companion; only the third looks up. Whether anyone climbs past the second rung, I admit, is not settled by argument. It is settled by lives.
